book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint

chapters.relation: Dirk Dunbar, a former professional player, argues that Daoist concepts illuminate basketball excellence and that the sport can be a path to the Dao. Balancing yin and yang means blending competition with surrender and strategy with spontaneity; Zhuangzi's archer shows how craving victory drains power. Wuwei explains the 'zone' of effortless play Dunbar experienced while scoring sixty-five points in a high school game and seventy-four in Iceland, while qi grounds free-throw breathing and visualization and ziran the discipline of releasing a shot without willing it in. Drawing on Daode jing verses and Phil Jackson's Sacred Hoops, he claims basketball teaches a life of disciplined surrender beyond the ego.

Bernard Jackson Jr. argues that basketball is an institution where black manhood is socially constructed (leaning on Naomi Zack's feminist point that gender identity is imposed by social designation), and that love among black players is essential to that construction while toughness is equivocal - the 'soft' label stuck to the gentlemanly David Robinson even as the Pistons walked off without congratulating the Bulls. Reading the documentary Hoop Dreams, he shows Arthur Agee and William Gates being used as commodities by recruiters, Coach Pingatore, and family expectations, invoking Marx on exploitation and 'use value' (Spike Lee's Nike-camp speech) and Kant's demand that persons be treated as ends, never merely as means. He likens William Gates's return to Chicago's Cabrini-Green as a minister to Plato's enlightened prisoner going back down into the cave.

The Wallaces argue that both the detractors (Stacey Pressman's claim that women's basketball 'sucks') and the admirers (John Wooden's 'purest basketball' praise) judge the women's game by patriarchal standards drawn from the men's game. Using Sandra Bartky's feminist extension of Foucault, they show how the female body was disciplined under male surveillance - early rule changes split the court and banned stealing to protect 'femininity', while players deflected the 'Amazon' charge with beauty pageants, revealing uniforms, and the Playboy offer to Lisa Harrison. The modern WNBA of Lisa Leslie and Michelle Snow, who can dunk but choose team play, points to a new game that escapes the feminine/masculine dichotomy instead of measuring women against men.

Kevin Kinghorn asks why practice stars like Kentucky's Josh Carrier suddenly choke in games and argues, via Bernard Williams's 'Deciding to Believe', that a player cannot simply choose to believe her next shot will go in: beliefs aim at truth, so a belief known to be self-chosen would not be a belief at all, any more than a mapmaker could 'choose' where to put Florida. Instead, desire and fear shape belief indirectly - Francis Bacon's 'whatever a man wishes were true, that he more readily believes' explains Larry Bird's unshakeable confidence, while fear of being the goat (Fred Brown's 1982 pass, Chris Webber's timeout) sabotages the underconfident. The practical strategies are to stockpile evidence of success through goals and visualization, or to remove the feared consequences of missing, as Rick Pitino did by publicly promising Kenny Walker he would stay a Knick as long as he kept shooting.

chapters.file: ch28 - The Hot Hand in Basketball.md
chapters.relation: Steven Hales rebuts the Gilovich-Vallone-Tversky studies (and Stephen Jay Gould) claiming that hot hands in basketball are statistical illusions. He dismantles their three skeptical arguments - 'success doesn't breed success' (76ers data), the demand for statistically improbable streaks (Joe DiMaggio's 56-game hitting streak), and the chance argument about run frequencies - showing each rests on an arbitrary, unprincipled cutoff for how 'hot' a streak must be, in the classic skeptical pattern of setting knowledge standards impossibly high. He then defends a commonsense definition on which a hot hand just is any run of above-average shooting: Wilt Chamberlain's thirty-five straight makes made him genuinely hot even if no one could feel the streak ending, and fans' and players' widespread judgments are vindicated rather than error-theorized away.

Tim Elcombe uses Dewey's pragmatist account of lived experience to read the Hoosiers scene in Butler Fieldhouse: Coach Dale's tape measure shows time and space are durable constants (the basket is ten feet in Indianapolis too), yet the awestruck Huskers will live that same space in a radically new way, and Kant and Augustine frame the gap between clock time and lived time. He argues basketball is the most 'phenomenal' game because the ticking clock creates genuine drama (Reggie Miller's 1995 buzzer three, childhood 'buzzer beater' games) and the ten-foot basket builds a vertical dimension no other sport matches, answering Scott Kretchmar's defense of event-regulated baseball. Our cultural obsession with dunking - Michael Jordan's Nike ads, Teen Wolf, Like Mike, White Men Can't Jump - expresses the human fascination with briefly defying gravity, a 'moving image of eternity'.

chapters.file: ch30 - Playing for the Same Team Again.md
chapters.relation: A fictional five-day phone dialogue between Michael Jordan and Phil Jackson works through the metaphysics of team identity before Jordan's 1995 comeback: qualitative versus numerical sameness, necessary and sufficient conditions ('same players, same positions'), Heraclitus's river, and whether the Bulls survive gradual turnover. The Ship of Theseus becomes the 'Boars' puzzle - the original five reassembled on an expansion team versus the continuous, degenerate Chicago roster - with Hobbes's two-ship twist, alongside the Minneapolis Lakers' move and a Bulls-Pistons gradual player swap. The resolution distinguishes the group (which persists by composition or continuity) from the team, which 'counts as' the Bulls only partly through fans' allegiance, echoing Searle's social reality; Jordan concludes he was asking the wrong question, and Aristotle's circular account of virtue supplies the model for circular criteria of loyal fandom.

chapters.file: ch31 - Plato and Aristotle on the Role of Soul in Taking the Rock to the Hole.md
chapters.relation: Daniel Gallagher reads Patrick Sparks's 2005 Elite Eight free-throw clank and miracle buzzer-beater through Plato's tripartite soul: the rational part failed at the line but the spirited part carried the off-balance game-tying three, while the Republic's three classes map onto basketball's workers (Steve Nash's passes), warriors (Dennis Rodman's rebounding), and rulers (John Stockton's leadership). Aristotle's four character types structure learning a jump shot - vicious, weak, self-controlled, and finally virtuous, as reason and inclination harmonize through repetition ('we are what we repeatedly do') - and the golden mean governs shot selection between the ball hog and the compulsive passer, with Michael Jordan as the player whose habituated instincts find the mean. Against Kantian armchair ethics, the jump shot and Kareem's sky hook were discovered by trial and error: virtuous performers set the standard, and we become good shooters by watching and imitating them.

chapters.file: ch32 - The Basket That Never Was.md
chapters.relation: Thomas Flint's thought experiment - a conference-championship buzzer-beater waved off because the clock expired, with inconclusive video - asks whether South Shore 'really' scored. He rejects the 'Goofy View' that game facts are referee-independent, since it would entail that only he and his camcorder-owning boss know who won any game ever (imperiling even Michael Jordan's 1982 title and Pistol Pete's scoring record) and would poison a coach's duty to teach rule-following when officials miss traveling. He also rejects the 'Tyranny of the Zebras' that makes officials infallible like the pope, since NCAA replay rules presuppose fallibility, and settles on officials as contest judges who award points: without the verdict no points exist, yet a blown call remains a genuine mistake in failing to apply the rules properly.

chapters.file: ch33 - Hoosiers and the Meaning of Life.md
chapters.relation: Michael Peterson argues that Hoosiers is a microcosm of life's meaning: Aristotle's eudaimonia frames the characters' searches (Norman Dale rebuilding his career, Shooter his self-esteem and his bond with son Everett), and Dale's 'in my book, we're going to be winners' speech shows that character, unselfish teamwork, and playing to potential - virtue learned by doing, as coaching models moral instruction - matter more than the scoreboard against South Bend Central. The film's second chances (Principal Summers's clean slate, Whit's return, Dale's hiring of the town drunk Shooter) reveal that character alone is insufficient: mercy and forgiveness, which Hannah Arendt traces to Jesus, reframe an unchangeable past and open a future. Peterson then surveys worldviews - naturalism (Bertrand Russell's 'accidental collocations of atoms'), postmodernism (Derrida's deconstruction), Hinduism's Atman-Brahman - and argues only Christian theism, in which God's nature is love (Aquinas), can ground the character and forgiveness the film dramatizes.

holes.name: Doxastic Voluntarism (deciding to believe)
holes.what: The thesis that we can choose what to believe; Bernard Williams's 'Deciding to Believe' argues against it because beliefs aim at truth, so a self-chosen belief would not be a belief.
holes.why: Chapter 27's core argument is that an underconfident shooter cannot simply choose to believe her next shot will go in, which is precisely the rejection of doxastic voluntarism.

holes.name: The Hot Hand Fallacy (misperception of randomness)
holes.what: The claim (Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky) that shooting streaks are ordinary chance runs and that players and fans misperceive patterns in random sequences.
holes.why: Chapter 28's skeptics ground their denial of hot hands in this fallacy claim, and Hales's entire chapter is a philosophical rebuttal of it.

holes.name: Institutional Facts (The Construction of Social Reality)
holes.what: Searle's account of facts that exist only through collective acceptance ('X counts as Y in context C'), such as money, presidencies, and teams.
holes.why: Chapter 30 resolves the same-team puzzle by separating the player group from the team, which 'counts as' the Bulls only relative to what the fans think.

holes.name: Constitutive Rules (rules that create the game)
holes.what: Rules that do not merely regulate a pre-existing activity but create the activity and its facts (points, strikes, goals), so that such facts exist only inside the rule system.
holes.why: Chapter 32's dispute over whether a waved-off basket 'really' scored turns on scoring facts being created by the rules and officials' awards rather than independently recorded.
